title: Polymorphism
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and core rule of polymorphism using at least one example.
Trace or adapt a minimal C++ example related to polymorphism and state its expected result.
Identify one precondition, error case, lifetime issue, portability assumption or version constraint relevant to the topic.

content.intro: Polymorphism focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.
content.why_it_matters: Polymorphism matters because exercise construction, mutation and destruction, and prefer composition when it expresses the relationship without an inheritance hierarchy. Connect this lesson to the earlier module prerequisites and use it as a building block rather than an isolated term.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
Classes combine state and operations behind an interface. Encapsulation protects invariants, and polymorphism is useful when runtime substitution is a real requirement.

Polymorphism focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.

Exercise construction, mutation and destruction, and prefer composition when it expresses the relationship without an inheritance hierarchy.

content_blocks.title: Minimal example: Polymorphism
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as `example.cpp`. Compile using `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic example.cpp -o example; then run ./example (Windows: .\example.exe).` The CodeLeaf page shows reference output only; it does not execute C++ learner code.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the example, rebuild with the same standard and warning flags, and rerun the same input. If the example is nondeterministic or depends on platform support, record that constraint instead of expecting byte-for-byte identical output.
content_blocks.limitations: The built-in CodeLeaf page does not execute C++ in a sandbox. Compile local teaching examples only; arbitrary learner code requires a separately deployed isolated runner with CPU, memory, process, filesystem and network limits.
content_blocks.explanation: The base interface uses a pure virtual function and virtual destructor. Calls through Shape references dispatch to the most-derived area implementation.

items.title: Compile-Time Polymorphism
items.text: Polymorphism lets one interface represent multiple concrete behaviors; virtual dispatch requires correct class design and usually a virtual base destructor for polymorphic deletion.

content_blocks.title: Guided practice
content_blocks.text: Before changing the example, predict the output and name the rule that produces it. Then modify one line to demonstrate compile-time polymorphism, and add a test for one boundary or failure scenario. Keep the experiment small enough that another learner can reproduce it.

content_blocks.title: Version, safety and portability note
content_blocks.text: Use standard C++ rather than compiler-specific behavior unless the lesson explicitly labels the dependency. Feature support varies by compiler version and standard-library implementation. Check the references and prefer explicit diagnostics to assumptions.

content.task: Extend the example for Polymorphism with one additional valid case and one boundary or failure case. State your expected result first, then compile with the documented C++20 warning flags.
task_acceptance_criteria: The code compiles in the documented standard mode with warnings enabled.
The predicted output matches the actual result for the added case.
One relevant boundary, lifetime, portability or error case is tested or documented.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming one successful example proves every case.
common_mistakes.why: It may miss an invalid input, boundary, error path or implementation difference.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the preconditions and test at least one ordinary case plus an edge or failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a language feature without checking its requirements.
common_mistakes.why: The code may depend on a standard version, an object lifetime or an API precondition.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the explicit standard mode and verify the relevant rule and compiler/library support.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring compiler diagnostics or simplifying away ownership and error behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Warnings and explicit contracts often expose a defect before it becomes a runtime problem.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with warnings, keep the smallest reproducible sample and state what happens when an operation fails.
